blocks.text: The loose cable was gone from the floor.

Laura noticed it before she noticed Daniel. It now ran beneath the trolley, along the wall and into the socket where the work lamp had been plugged in. Daylight through the high windows fell across the glass cylinder.
Her photograph had been moved off the bench. In its place stood a shallow iron tray, black with old scorch marks.
Daniel emerged from behind the tank carrying a folded cloth.
“You came back.”
“You said you'd have something to show me.”
He put the cloth beneath one wheel of the trolley and pressed his shoe against it. The machine stopped rocking.

Luke hovered above the open control box. He had been watching Daniel work since before the daylight reached the windows. For most of that time, his uncle had answered questions without looking up. Now he was wiping his glasses.
Laura took off her coat and laid it on a clear part of the bench.
The cylinder was still empty. Three copper coils ran around it. The brass funnel caught a bright reflection from the doorway, but nothing inside the glass glowed.
Daniel closed the control box and tightened its two front screws.

He wheeled the collector away from the benches, checked the length of the lead and turned it until the funnel faced a clear stretch of concrete. Beyond the other end, he set the iron tray on a low stand.
Laura watched him move a box of oily rags well out of the way. She waited until he had finished before taking the place he indicated.
“Small,” he said.
She gave him a look.
“I'm familiar with small.”
Daniel stepped to the side of the trolley. Luke drifted after him, keeping clear of the funnel.
Laura could see the inside of it from where she stood. The dark circle at its center was larger than the holes she had made in the baking sheet. She fixed her eyes on that circle.
Daniel turned a switch.
A low hum came from beneath the glass. The cylinder remained clear.
His glasses had slipped down his nose again. He pushed them back, glanced at the meters and raised one finger.
Laura spat.
The orange streak crossed the space between her and the funnel. A brief glow filled the brass mouth. Through the glass, she saw a thread of light bend toward the nearest coil.
Something struck the tray with a sharp hiss.
Daniel leaned toward the meters.
One needle lifted.
blocks.alt: Laura spits a small orange plasma shot into the collector’s brass intake as Daniel watches a meter rise and bodyless Luke observes from the side.

blocks.text: He did not say anything.
The needle trembled above its resting place, dropped a little, then held. Inside the cylinder, a faint orange glow remained between the coils.
Laura kept her mouth closed. She waited for Daniel to announce that the needle had stuck or that they needed to try again.
He bent closer to the glass instead.
Luke came down until he could see the meter beneath his uncle's elbow.
“It moved,” he said.
Daniel turned his head.
“I saw.”
The needle held.
A spot on the iron tray still glowed where the residue had landed. Laura looked from it to the light inside the cylinder. Her spit had not simply passed through.
Daniel lifted his glasses and rubbed the bridge of his nose. When he put them back on, he was smiling.
Luke stayed beside the meter.

He had seen needles move before. Daniel's old instruments had twitched when a door slammed or a cable was pulled loose. This one had risen with the orange flash and stayed above the little mark at the bottom.
Daniel switched the machine off.
The hum faded. The light inside the cylinder became dimmer but did not disappear.
Luke looked up sharply.
“It's still there.”
“Some of it,” Daniel said.
He made a note on the paper beside the control box. For once, Luke could look at the machine and see what his uncle was writing about.
blocks.alt: Luke studies the raised collector needle and the faint captured glow with renewed hope while Daniel records the successful result.

blocks.text: He remembered fastening the buttons of a shirt. He could not have said why that particular thing came to him: his thumb pushing one button through a stubborn hole, his other hand holding the cloth steady.
He had hurried through it every morning.
Daniel reached for the screwdriver.
“Other drawer,” Luke said.
His uncle paused, opened the drawer Luke had indicated and found it beneath a packet of washers.
Luke moved to the far side of the trolley. From there, he could see both the cylinder and the meter without Daniel's shoulder blocking them.
“If you try it again, I can watch this side.”
Daniel glanced toward him.
“All right.”
Luke settled at the height of the glass. He did not look toward Laura.
She had heard the change in his voice anyway. The little head that had challenged every step she took through the workshop was now making room for the experiment.
Laura moved nearer the glass. The orange light flickered between the coils, familiar from the face she had watched above the lake.
“That's what he's made of,” Daniel said.
She studied the captured plasma. “How much can it hold?”
Daniel looked at the narrow space the needle had crossed. “We've only just begun.”
Laura picked up her coat.
She pictured the flame over the lake. The certainty with which he hovered out of reach, telling her there were things they could work on. He would have to look at the meter too.
Luke was still on the other side of the glass, studying the captured glow. For once, she let him stay there without a remark.
Daniel knelt beside the trolley with a piece of chalk.
blocks.alt: Daniel kneels to mark the collector trolley’s position on the floor while Laura considers the approach and Luke watches the machine.

blocks.text: He marked the floor beside one wheel, then looked along the cylinder toward the place where Laura had stood. He put a second mark nearer the brass mouth.
Laura draped her coat over one arm and came to see.
“The shot came to us,” he said. “He won't.”
Luke rose above the trolley. His eyes moved between the chalk marks.
Daniel rubbed out the farther one with his shoe.

A small shot had crossed several feet because Laura had aimed it. The collector had caught energy at its mouth. Nothing they had done showed that it could reach across a street and pull a flying flame out of the sky.
Laura looked at the nearer mark.
“He'll have to come close.”
“Yes.”
Daniel put the chalk on the trolley rail and stood.

The workshop was quiet enough now that Laura could hear a truck passing outside. Beyond the loading entrance, ordinary people were going somewhere, carrying parcels, hurrying for buses. None of them knew what was sitting in this room.
She touched the flame pattern along her side.
Daniel followed the movement, then looked toward the funnel again.
“We need a place where he'll come to you,” he said.
Laura looked down at the little mark on the concrete.
This time, she could imagine him there.
